prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The five depth frames show a steep rock face surrounding a narrow, uneven ledge, with foreground rock and equipment roughly 0.3–1 m from the camera wearer and the main wall about 1–4 m away. In frames 1–2, the hanging rope is near the camera and extends upward out of view; nearby lower-edge shapes are partly cropped, while no other person is clearly depth-separated. In frame 3, about five people stand roughly 2–5 m ahead and close together, generally within about 0.5–1.5 m of one another; in frame 4, another group of roughly five is about 2–4 m ahead, with several bodies mutually occluding and the rightmost person slightly farther back. Frame 5 opens toward a more distant rock slope, with a small person high and ahead at roughly 8–15 m and a rope descending toward the camera; these metric estimates are highly uncertain because the map is monocular, has bright washed-out foreground regions, and assigns inconsistent depth across similarly distant rock surfaces.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map isolates one partly cropped person near the lower-left area of frame 2, two clusters of about five people in frames 3 and 4, and isolated detections in frame 5, making people easier to separate from the similarly colored rock than in RGB. In frame 3, the people are aligned across the ledge about 2–5 m in front of the wearer, with overlapping masks indicating separations often below about 1 m; in frame 4, the cluster lies mostly center-right, with people side-by-side and partly in front of one another, while one additional mask sits lower and farther right. The masks suggest several figures are turned sideways or partly toward the wearer, but they do not reliably determine gaze, front-versus-back orientation, or exact distance; only adjacent people appear within one another's arm reach, and no clearly segmented person is within the wearer's arm reach. Reliability is poor at the strip edges and at long range: masks are truncated, some labels overlap or are clipped, much of the rope and rock is unsegmented, and the distant frame-5 climber appears labeled as a person while another tiny mark is implausibly labeled bird.
descriptions.pose: The pose map detects only one person, in frame 4 near the center-right, roughly 2–4 m in front of the camera wearer and amid the nearby group. The skeleton shows a mostly upright body with bent, raised arms extending toward the left side of the image and legs descending below, so nearby people or rock may lie within that person's arm reach, but hand positions and contact are not resolved. Its joint geometry provides limb orientation and body extent that are difficult to read against the rock in RGB, yet it does not establish gaze direction or confidently show whether the torso faces toward, away from, or sideways to the wearer. It misses all other visible people across frames 2–5, including mutually occluded group members and the distant climber, and several detected joints appear compressed or displaced, so changes such as approach, retreat, and turning cannot be tracked reliably.
